entries.modern_form: PIE *mórǵ-s / *mereǵ- 'edge, boundary, border' (Pokorny 738 mereg-; AHD merg-)
entries.note: Pokorny p. 738 has the root in exactly these words — 'mereg- ‚Rand, Grenze‘' — with Npers. marz, Lat. margō, Goth. marka, OIr. mruig as its members; Watkins/AHD gives 'merg-. Boundary, border' with the cross-reference '[Pok. mereg- 738.]'. Nourai's two shapes 'Merg / Mereg' answer to Pokorny's *merg-/*mereg- notation, and Wiktionary reconstructs the underlying noun as *mórǵ-s (obl. *m̥ rǵ-) 'edge, boundary, border'. Language label ('Indo-European') and gloss ('mark, border') are both right, and all six nodes on the chart are members of the standard cognate set, so the whole entry stands. Two refinements a modern reader should add: (i) Walde-Pokorny II 283 (1927) had not yet made this a root of its own — it filed the border-words under the 'streichen, streifen' root and called their membership 'zweifelhaft' on vowel grounds; Pokorny 1959 separated them, which is the view followed today (Wiktionary's *mórǵ-s cautiously adds 'possibly derived from the verb underlying Hittite mārki “to divide, separate”'). (ii) The 'mark = sign' sense of the Germanic branch is secondary to 'boundary'; see node #3. The extraction is faithful to the printed page (pdf 337, copied to data/verification/sources/refs/ocr/BOOK/337.png).
entries.note_fa: ریشة هندواروپایی آغازین *mórǵ-s / *mereǵ- «کناره، مرز» درست و پذیرفته است؛ پوکورنی در ص ۷۳۸ دقیقاً همین را «mereg- ‚Rand, Grenze‘» می‌آورد و فارسی «مرز»، لاتینی margō و گوتی marka را زیر آن می‌نشاند؛ واتکینز (AHD) نیز همین را «merg-. Boundary, border» ثبت کرده است. نامِ زبان (هندواروپایی) و معنا («نشان، مرز») هر دو صحیح است و هر شش گرهِ نمودار از اعضای شناختة این خانواده‌اند. دو نکتة تکمیلی: والده-پوکورنی (ج ۲ ص ۲۸۳) در ۱۹۲۷ این واژه‌ها را زیر ریشة «ساییدن» می‌آورد و پیوستگی آنها را «مشکوک» می‌خواند، و جداکردنِ آن از پوکورنی ۱۹۵۹ است؛ دیگر آنکه معنای «نشان» در شاخة ژرمنی ثانوی است و از «مرز» پدید آمده است.

nodes.derivation: Young Avestan marəza- m. 'march, border district', attested at Vendīdād 3.5 (Bartholomae, AiW col. 1153: 'Mark, Grenzgebiet'). Nourai's spelling 'mereza' is simply the older Western transliteration of marəza-, with schwa written e — Horn 1893 (no. 974) prints 'merezu' and Klein 'marǟza', so the form is not corrupt. It goes back to Proto-Iranian *marȜa(h)- from PIE *mórǵ-s 'edge, boundary': PIE palatal *ǵ gives Avestan z by the satem shift, against the plain g of Latin margō and Germanic *markō. One caution the chart does not make: this marəza- 'border' (AiW 1153) is a different word from the homonymous Avestan verb marəz- 'to graze, touch' (AiW 1152), the source of MP marz- 'copulate' (Nyberg s.v. marzihistan) — the two are constantly confused.
nodes.derivation_fa: اوستایی marəza- «مرز، ناحیة سرحدی» در وندیداد ۳؛۵ آمده است (بارتولومه، ستون ۱۱۵۳). نگارش «mereza» در کتاب خطا نیست؛ شیوة کهنِ اروپایی است که شوای میانگی (ə) را e می‌نوشته‌اند — هرن هم «merezu» می‌نویسد. این واژه از ایرانی باستان *marȜa- و آن از هندواروپایی آغازین *mórǵ-s است؛ *ǵ کامی در زبان‌های ستم (اوستایی) به z بدل شده، در برابر g در لاتینی margō. هشدار: این marəza- را باید از همآوایِ آن، ستاک marəz- «ساییدن، لمس کردن» (ستون ۱۱۵۲، منشأ marz- پهلوی)، جدا دانست. ادعای نورایی درست است.

nodes.derivation: NP مرز marz 'border, boundary; strip of land between fields' continues Middle Persian marz [mlc] 'boundary, march; (astronomical) term' (MacKenzie, CPD s.v.) < Old Iranian *marza- = Av. marəza-. The development is trivially regular: the cluster -rz is stable from Old Iranian through Middle to New Persian, so marza- > marz > marz with only loss of the thematic vowel. The derivative marzbān 'margrave, warden of the marches' (MP marz-pān, Kārnāmag 39) proves the word's currency in Sasanian administration and was itself lent onward to Armenian marzpan, Syriac marzbānā and Arabic marzubān. Mo'in's own etymological footnote at Borhan-e Qāte' p. 1986 — Nourai's cited page — gives exactly this chain (Av. marəza- 'frontier of a country' > Pahl. marz, marz-bān > NP marz), with Gothic marka and Latin margo as cognates.
nodes.derivation_fa: «مرز» فارسی نو بازماندة فارسی میانة marz «مرز، سرحد، اصطلاح نجومی» (مکنزی) و آن از ایرانی باستان *marza- همانندِ اوستایی marəza- است. دگرگونی آوایی ناچیز است: خوشة پایانی -rz در همة دوره‌ها پایدار مانده و فقط واکة ستاکی افتاده است. مشتقِ «مرزبان» (پهلوی marz-pān، کارنامه ۳۹) به ارمنی marzpan، سریانی و عربی «مرزبان» وام داده شده است. معین در حاشیة برهان قاطع (ص ۱۹۸۶) دقیقاً همین زنجیره را می‌آورد؛ ادعای نورایی درست است.

nodes.derivation: Proto-Germanic *markō f. 'boundary, border territory' < PIE *mórǵ-s: Gothic marka 'Grenze', OHG marc(h)a 'Grenze, Grenzland', OE mearc, ON mǫrk 'borderland, forest' (forests served as frontiers) — all listed at Pokorny 738. Nourai's gloss 'to mark' belongs strictly to the denominative verbs built on that noun, PGmc *markōn / *markjan (OE mearcian 'to make a mark', OHG merken 'to note'): a boundary was established by walking it and setting boundary-posts, so 'boundary' > 'boundary-post, landmark' > 'sign' > 'to make a sign'. Watkins states the double value in one breath: 'Germanic *mark-, boundary, border territory; also to mark out a boundary by walking around it (ceremonially “beating the bounds”); also a landmark, boundary marker, and a mark in general'. So the node is right, with the noun logically prior to the verb.

nodes.derivation: Three reflexes of the same Germanic noun, but by two different routes. mark n. is direct inheritance: ME merke, marke < OE mearc 'boundary, sign, mark', whose sense-history runs 'boundary' > 'boundary post' > 'sign in general' > 'visible trace' (Etymonline; 'any visible trace or impression' by c. 1200). march 'border, frontier' (13th c., whence the Welsh Marches) is a re-import: Frankish *marka gave Old French marche 'border country', borrowed into ME as marche — Skeat: 'march (1). a border, frontier … A.S. mearc, a mark, boundary'; Watkins files MARCH¹ and MARCH² under merg- via 'Old French marc, marche' and Frankish *markōn. remark (17th c.) is F. remarquer = re- + marquer, and OF marquer/merchier is itself a Germanic loan (Klein: 'OF. merchier, ‘to mark, note’, is a Teut. loan word'), from PGmc *markja- (ON merki). So the arrow Germanic > English is right in substance for all three; two of them travelled through French, which the chart does not show.

nodes.derivation: Latin margō, gen. marginis 'edge, brink, border, margin' is the Italic member of the family, formed with an -n- stem extension on PIE *mórǵ- (Pokorny writes '*m̥ rǵ-en-'). Its plain velar g — against Avestan marəza-, Persian marz with z — is exactly the centum treatment of PIE palatal *ǵ, which is what makes this cognate set a standard textbook example. Pokorny 738 puts 'lat. margö, -inis „Rand, Grenze“' immediately after Npers. marz; Watkins gives 'Latin margo, border, edge: MARGIN' as branch 4 of merg-. Latin has no verb from the base, which has led some (de Vaan) to suspect a Celtic or Germanic loan into Latin, but nobody disputes the etymological connection itself.

nodes.derivation: ME margine (late 14th c., Chaucer's era, first of the blank edge of a page) < Latin marginem, the accusative of margō; as usual for Latin -o/-inis nouns the English form is built on the oblique stem (cf. virgin < virginem, origin < originem). Etymonline: 'from Latin marginem (nominative margo) “edge, brink, border, margin,” from PIE root *merg- “boundary, border”'. Klein s.v. marge/margin agrees ('F., fr. L. margo, gen. marginis'), and Watkins ends the merg- article with 'Latin margo …: MARGIN'. The financial and figurative senses ('margin of profit', 'marginal') are 19th-c. metaphors on the page-edge sense.

entries.modern_form: PIE *merk͝- 'to grasp, seize' (Pokorny 739); but the Latin merx-family is usually assigned to a separate Italic root merk- 'commerce', possibly Etruscan (Watkins merk-²)
entries.note: The root box itself is accurate as far as it goes: Pokorny p. 739 does have 'merk͝- ‚fassen, ergreifen‘' (Skt. mṛśáti 'touches, takes hold', Gk. márptō, Gk. hárptis 'robber'), so the language label and the gloss 'to take, grasp' are right. What is doubtful is the whole tree Nourai hangs from it. Pokorny himself attaches the Latin family only with a caveat — 'fraglich ist Zugehörigkeit von lat. merx ‚Ware‘, merces, -edis … mercārī ‚handeln‘'. Watkins goes further and lists the commerce words as a separate BRACKETED root, his notation for a non-Indo-European item: '[merk-2. Italic root, possibly from Etruscan, referring to aspects of commerce … [In Pok. merk- 739.]]'. Ernout-Meillet: 'merx … sans étymologie i.-e. sûre'; Klein: 'merx … which is of uncertain origin'; de Vaan reconstructs only Proto-Italic *merks and suspects an Etruscan source for the whole economic stem (Mercurius included). Against that, recent work has tried to make merx Indo-European again after all: Nikolaev derives it from *merkʷ- with Gk. márptō and Tocharian A märk- 'take away' — essentially Nourai's arrow — while Matasović would instead attach it to *merǵ- 'to divide', i.e. to the root of the preceding entry on this very page. So 'plausible': a defensible minority position, not the consensus. Verdicts below are given per node accordingly.
entries.note_fa: خودِ ریشه درست است: پوکورنی در ص ۷۳۹ ریشة *merk͝- «گرفتن، چنگ زدن» را با سنسکریت mṛśáti و یونانی márptō می‌آورد؛ پس برچسب و معنا صحیح است. اما پیوستنِ خانوادة لاتینی merx به این ریشه محلّ تردید است: خودِ پوکورنی آن را «fraglich» می‌خواند، واتکینز آن را ریشة جداگانة ایتالیکی و احتمالاً اتروسکی می‌شمارد (در کروشه، که نشانة غیرهندواروپایی بودن است)، و ارنو-میه و کلاین و دووان آن را «بی‌ریشة مطمئن» می‌دانند. در مقابل، پژوهش‌های تازه (نیکولایف) باز ریشة *merkʷ- را با همان معنای «گرفتن» بازسازی کرده‌اند. پس ادعای نورایی با احتیاط پذیرفتنی است، نه رای غالب.

nodes.derivation: Latin merx, gen. mercis f. 'wares, merchandise' is genuine and old (Plautus, Cistellaria 727 'bona mers, era, haec et callida est'; Ernout-Meillet 'Ancien, usuel'). 'comerx' however is not a Latin word at all: Nourai has compressed con- + merx, i.e. commercium 'trade' (Klein s.v. commerce: 'L. commercium … fr. con- and merx, gen. mercis'), into a pseudo-nominative. The printed page (pdf 337) really does show 'merx, comerx : merchandise', so this is the book's own shorthand/misprint and the extraction is faithful. On the derivation itself: Pokorny does file the family here — p. 739 under merk͝- 'fassen, ergreifen' — but explicitly with 'fraglich ist Zugehörigkeit von lat. merx'. Watkins brackets merk-² as an 'Italic root, possibly from Etruscan'; Ernout-Meillet: 'merx … sans étymologie i.-e. sûre'; Klein: 'merx … which is of uncertain origin'. In the 2020s Nikolaev has argued for a real PIE *merkʷ- linking merx to Gk. márptō 'take hold' and Toch. A märk- 'take away', which would vindicate Nourai's arrow — so the derivation is plausible, only the second form is spurious.

nodes.derivation: The Italian word for 'commerce' is commercio (plural commerci); the box prints the plural as if it were the headword, and the page image confirms 'commerci : commerce' is what the book set, so the extraction is faithful. Italian commercio is a learned (dotta) borrowing straight from Latin commercium (con- + merx), not a popular development — the inherited Italian member of the family is mercato < Lat. mercātus (Klein s.v. market: 'whence also It. mercato …'). The arrow Latin merx > Italian is therefore unobjectionable in itself. What the node cannot bear is the weight the chart puts on it: its reference MON:3392 is Mo'in's گمرک article, which tags the Persian word simply '[مأخوذ از ترکی]' (from Turkish) and knows nothing of an Italian step.

nodes.derivation: There is no Portuguese *cumerx. Portuguese for 'trade' is comércio, a learned loan from Lat. commercium (the inherited member being mercado < mercātus, cf. Klein s.v. market 'Sp. and Port. mercado'). Nor is Portuguese the channel by which the word reached Persian: Lokotsch no. 751 gives the real route — 'Tk. gümrük: ‚Zoll‘ [aus gr. κομμέρκιον, lat. commercium]' — and Hobson-Jobson p. 384, which Nourai himself cites on the child node, says the same: gumruk 'is again, through Low Greek, from the Latin commercium'. κομμέρκιον was the Byzantine customs levy (a Latin administrative term taken into Greek in late antiquity), and it passed from Byzantine Greek into Ottoman Turkish, not through the Iberian trading languages. The printed page shows 'cumerx : trade', so the odd form is the book's, but the node itself has no place in the tree.
nodes.derivation_fa: در پرتغالی واژه‌ای به صورت *cumerx وجود ندارد؛ «تجارت» در پرتغالی comércio است، وام‌واژه‌ای عالمانه از commercium. مهم‌تر آنکه راهِ رسیدن این واژه به فارسی پرتغالی نبوده است: لوکوتش (شمارة ۷۵۱) و خودِ مأخذِ نورایی (هابسن-جابسن ص ۳۸۴) می‌گویند که ترکی gümrük از یونانی بیزانطینی κομμέρκιον گرفته شده و آن خود از لاتینی commercium است. پژوهش امروزی این گره را رد می‌کند؛ صورتِ چاپی نیز خطای خود کتاب است.

nodes.derivation: Two unrelated words are put in one box. (a) گمرک gomrok 'customs, customs duty/house' is a Turkish loan: Ottoman Turkish گمرك gümrük < Byzantine Greek κομμέρκιον kommérkion (the Byzantine customs levy) < Latin commercium; Mo'in tags the Persian word '[مأخوذ از ترکی]' and Dehkhoda dates the Turkish adoption to after the conquest of Constantinople (1453), whence Persian; Lokotsch 751 gives the identical chain with Bulg. gumruk, Serb. džumruk as parallel borrowings. Nourai's ultimate Latin source is right, his Italian→Portuguese relay is not, and the phonetics confirm it: Greek/Turkish gü- for Latin co(m)- and the -ük ending are Turkish, whereas an Italian or Portuguese loan would have kept -io/-cio. (b) گمبرون Gambroon/Gombroon, the European name of the port Shah ʿAbbās renamed Bandar ʿAbbās in 1622, is a place-name, and Nourai's own cited page rejects the customs etymology for it: Hobson-Jobson p. 384 reports the 'Turkish for custom-house' story and answers 'But this etymology of the name seems hardly probable', preferring Pers. kamrūn / Port. camarão 'shrimp' after A. Hamilton (1727), who says the Portuguese named the fishing village so 'in Derision, because it was a good place for catching Prawns and Shrimps, which they call Camerong'. Early European spellings — Gamrun, Comorão (1614), Cummeroon, Gamron — point the same way. So the node is disputed on both halves.

nodes.derivation: An unlabelled pass-through box standing for French merci. Latin mercēdem (acc. of mercēs) > Old French mercit, then merci f. 'reward, gift; kindness, grace, pity' (11th–12th c.), by the regular loss of the Latin post-tonic syllable and palatalisation of -c- before the front vowel. The semantic groundwork was already Latin: in Vulgar Latin mercēs meant 'favour, pity', and from the 6th c. Church Latin used it of 'the heavenly reward earned by those who show kindness to the helpless and those from whom no requital can be expected' (Etymonline s.v. mercy). Out of that 'favour owed' sense French merci became the formula of thanks. Klein s.v. mercy documents the same step: 'fr. OF. mercit, merci (F. merci), fr. L. mercedem'.

nodes.derivation: مرسی mersi 'thank you' is a direct modern loan from French merci, one of the large Francophone layer that entered Persian from the Qājār period on — the Dār al-Fonūn, French-educated officials and students, and (for polite formulas) salon usage; it is now fully colloquial beside ممنونم and متشکرم. Mo'in's entry, Nourai's cited page, tags it exactly so: «(مِ) [فر.] (فعل.) متشکرم، ممنونم», '[فر.]' being Mo'in's tag for French. Phonetically French [mɛʁsi] is taken over as mersi, the French uvular r rendered by Persian ر and the final -i as ی; Nourai's spelling 'mercî' is his own transcription habit (c for [s], î for final ī), not a Persian form. The node therefore closes a chain Latin mercēdem > OF merci > NP مرسی — a European loan, with no Arabic mediation.
